analysis.one_liner: Tightens safety rules for meatpacking plants, restricts punishing attendance policies, and slows fast line speeds.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Rep. Ro Khanna with 29 Democratic cosponsors, never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in five House committees until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required companies to get a federal safety certification before increasing slaughter line speeds, funded 60 million dollars a year for six years of additional workplace safety inspectors, banned "no-fault" attendance policies that penalize workers for legally protected leave, and required ergonomic, bathroom-access, and COVID/infectious-disease standards at meat and poultry plants. It also added anti-retaliation protections, a private right to sue, country-of-origin labeling for beef, pork, and dairy, and new antitrust-style rules restricting large meatpackers' contracts with ranchers and poultry growers. It never got a committee hearing or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Meat and poultry processing workers, who suffer injury and amputation rates well above the private-sector average and whose work was especially dangerous during the COVID-19 pandemic. The bill would have given them slower line speeds unless safety was certified, guaranteed bathroom access, ergonomic protections, faster injury reporting, strong retaliation protections, and the right to sue over unsafe conditions. It also would have helped ranchers and contract poultry farmers by curbing packers' use of opaque formula contracts and the poultry "tournament" pay system, and helped consumers by restoring country-of-origin labeling.

how_it_helps.text: It bars federal funds from being used to raise slaughter line speeds and blocks line-speed waivers unless an ergonomics evaluation certifies the increase would not harm worker safety — line speed is a recognized risk factor for lacerations and musculoskeletal injuries.

It appropriates $60 million per year for fiscal years 2024–2029 to hire additional OSHA inspectors and creates a permanent regional inspection program covering amputation hazards, ergonomics, line speeds, bathroom access, and chemical exposures.

It makes it an unlawful employment practice for employers to run 'no-fault' point-based attendance policies that punish workers for legally protected leave, with enforcement and remedies modeled on the Family and Medical Leave Act.

It requires OSHA to issue standards on ergonomics, prompt medical referrals, and infectious-disease exposure (including an emergency temporary COVID-19 standard within 7 days of enactment), and mandates verified access to toilet facilities with restrictions like sign-out keys or waiting lists.

It strengthens retaliation protections for meat and poultry workers — including a presumption of retaliation for adverse actions within 90 days of protected activity, protection from immigration-status threats, and a private right of action allowing workers to sue with compensatory and punitive damages.

It restricts packers' use of forward contracts without a firm base price, bans purchasing arrangements where the producer is not materially participating in management, prohibits the poultry tournament pay system when it uses factors outside the grower's control, and requires grant recipients to sign labor peace agreements and not sell to large packers for 10 years.
It restores mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork and extends it to dairy products, so shoppers can see where their meat and dairy come from.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking and poultry processing companies would bear the costs: slower or unraised line speeds, ergonomic and infectious-disease controls, more inspections, retaliation liability with damages, and compliance with attendance-policy rules. Agribusiness contractors would face limits on formula contracts and the tournament pay system, and retailers would face country-of-origin labeling requirements. Taxpayers fund the added inspectors and grants. Meat prices could rise slightly if slower line speeds raise processing costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes significant compliance costs on meat and poultry processors — ergonomic programs, infectious-disease exposure control plans, expanded inspections, and damages exposure under a new private right of action — costs that could be passed on to consumers through higher meat prices, and opponents would argue they burden an industry already operating on thin margins.

The attendance-policy subtitle applies far beyond meatpacking — to virtually any employer covered by Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, including states (whose sovereign immunity it waives) — a broad mandate that goes well beyond the bill's title and would add compliance obligations across the economy.

The bill directs OSHA to issue an emergency COVID-19 standard within 7 days and bypasses several normal rulemaking reviews (Regulatory Flexibility Act, Paperwork Reduction Act, Executive Orders 12866 and 13771), which critics would call rushed and legally vulnerable, especially since the public health emergency it responds to was already winding down by the time it was introduced.

Restoring mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork has previously drawn trade challenges from Canada and Mexico, and the Packers and Stockyards changes would restrict marketing tools (formula contracts, packer feeding) that some producers and economists defend as legitimate risk management.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to one of the most dangerous jobs in the country: the bill's own findings note meatpacking workers suffer double the private-sector amputation rate and musculoskeletal injuries that can exceed half of workers, conditions the bill attributes in part to line speeds and thin OSHA enforcement [S3]. The costs fall mostly on a small number of very large, profitable processing companies, with some possible pass-through to meat prices, and the attendance-policy rules reach a much broader set of employers than the bill's title suggests. The strongest fair criticism is breadth — the bill packs worker-safety, antitrust, labeling, and general employment policy into one vehicle — but the core worker-safety provisions are targeted at documented, specific hazards.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to five House committees and then to an Agriculture subcommittee, and no committee ever took it up or held a hearing before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, joined by five original cosponsors including Reps. Norton, Payne, Grijalva, Hayes, and Lee of California.

The same day, it was referred to the Agriculture Committee and, in addition, to the Education and the Workforce, Oversight, House Administration, and Judiciary Committees — five separate committees whose sign-off would be needed for the bill to move.
On March 2, 2023, it was referred to the Agriculture Committee's Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry; that was the last action ever taken on the bill.
The bill accumulated 29 cosponsors, all Democrats, but no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking and poultry processing companies are better off: they face no new line-speed limits, ergonomic standards, inspection expansion, retaliation liability, country-of-origin labeling, or contract restrictions on their dealings with ranchers and poultry growers.

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited five original cosponsors across five committees' jurisdictions.

for.name: 29 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill, none of them Republicans.

against.name: House Agriculture, Education and the Workforce, Oversight, House Administration, and Judiciary Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor, and the bill had no Republican cosponsors in a chamber whose committees the majority controlled.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 supporters (the sponsor and 29 cosponsors) were Democrats and no Republican signed on; no vote ever occurred, so the party split is visible only in sponsorship.

industries.industry: Large meatpacking and poultry processing companies
industries.note: The bill would cost them line-speed flexibility, ergonomic and infectious-disease compliance, more inspections, a private right of action with damages, and country-of-origin labeling duties. These companies profit from fast processing lines and thin inspection, and their cost is the safety gain for their own workforce.

industries.industry: Contract poultry growers and independent livestock producers
industries.note: The bill bars the poultry 'tournament' pay system when it uses factors outside growers' control, restricts opaque formula contracts and packer livestock ownership, and requires data transparency and jury rights for growers. These provisions shift bargaining power from a few large packers back toward producers.

Federal meat and poultry processing grants would require recipients to sign labor peace agreements that bar anti-union campaigns and provide union access to workers, and retaliation remedies could not be waived by collective bargaining or arbitration agreements.
Mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef, pork, and dairy adds labeling and recordkeeping costs, but delivers origin information shoppers have repeatedly said they want.
